Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Jake was seventeen when the hurricane came. He remembered the sound first—a deep, continuous roar like a train had parked itself outside his family’s first-floor apartment, then the sudden crack of the front door giving way. Water surged in, dark and cold, smelling of sewage and wet wood and something metallic. He had been in the hallway, and he scrambled into the bathroom, the only room without windows, and sat in the empty bathtub while the water rose to his knees. He pressed his palms against the porcelain and watched the line of water creep up the tile, counting seconds until his breath caught. That smell—the dense, damp mixture of mud and chemicals and decay—lodged itself somewhere behind his nose. He stayed in the tub for three hours until the water stopped rising, and when help came he had to be pulled out because his legs wouldn’t work.

Three years later, Jake was nineteen and working the fry station at a Burger King on the edge of town. He was a fast-food worker, and the job was supposed to be simple, but nothing felt simple anymore. The smell that came off the wet mop when the night crew cleaned the floors was the worst—it hit him sometimes when he was refilling the soda machine, and suddenly he was back in that bathroom, water up to his knees, the roar in his ears. The images would flash in his mind: the doorframe splintering, the line of water climbing the tile, the way the light turned gray as the window well filled. And with the images came the same raw terror he had felt that day, his heart slamming, his hands going cold. He learned to hold his breath when someone mopped nearby, to walk quickly past the bleach station, to never look at the drain in the floor.

He had also learned to avoid anything that could feel stressful—which was almost everything. Crowded rushes, angry customers, even friendly small talk with coworkers felt like a minefield. Before every shift he rehearsed the conversations he might have, silently mouthing the lines to himself in the break room: *“Can I take your order?” “Yes, please, the fries will be a few minutes.” “No, I don’t know when the manager will be back.”* He repeated them until they felt scripted, because unscripted interactions made his chest tighten. He rehearsed ordering coffee at the gas station, too, and calling his mother to check in. It was exhausting, but the alternative—saying something wrong, being caught off guard, feeling the panic spike—felt worse. He had tried not to think about the hurricane at all. He pushed the images down, turned up his music, stayed up late until his mind was too tired to drift. But the smells found him anyway, and the pictures came in the cracks between songs, and the terror returned no matter how hard he squeezed his eyes shut.

Jake could barely recognize the person he had become. Before the water, he had been a kid who laughed easily, who cracked jokes in the lunch line, who didn’t plan every sentence. That person felt like a stranger now. He saw photos of himself from before and felt a hollow ache—that kid was happy, and he was miserable, and he was certain the change was permanent. He had told himself a hundred times that he was broken, that the hurricane had rewired something inside him that could never be fixed. He walked through his days waiting for the next trigger, rehearsing, avoiding, suppressing, and the effort of it had hollowed him out.

What finally brought him to the clinic was his manager pulling him aside after a third week of poor marks on his shift evaluation. He had walked off the line twice because a cleaning chemical smell had triggered a wave of images, and he had started avoiding the busier shifts altogether, calling in sick or swapping with anyone who would trade. He knew he was losing ground—not just at work, but with himself. He came because he was terrified that the person he used to be was gone for good, but also because, underneath that, a small part of him hoped that maybe someone could show him how to live with the memories without drowning in them again.
